speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In my speech, I will, first, provide the background to the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will explain why we have assessed that it is necessary to proactively act to introduce these amendments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will, then, take Members through the details of the proposed amendments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In doing so, I will share how we carefully scoped the proposals to achieve a balance between the public interest in guarding against abuse of process and the rights of litigants to ventilate genuine claims before the Courts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The AOJPA consolidated the law of contempt of court, which was previously set out in multiple cases, in a single piece of legislation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The fundamental aim of our contempt of court laws is to protect our Courts and our justice system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The justice system is critical to Singapore's continued success.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: It benefits all of us in various ways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For example, our criminal justice system ensures law and order and a safe Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Our commercial law regime provides a stable platform for investment and economic growth and allows for the expedient resolution of commercial disputes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In the community sphere, we have set up specialised tribunals and introduced simplified judge-led processes, that allow for the effective resolution of community disputes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Our family justice system aims to find timely and enduring solutions to family disputes by applying therapeutic justice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The AOJPA protects the justice system across all these spheres.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The AOJPA has become even more important in recent years, as we have taken significant steps to improve access to justice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These steps include setting up the Protection from Harassment Court and the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunal (CDRT).

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These reforms provide simplified processes intended to allow Singaporeans to enforce their rights more easily.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Promoting access to justice is part of the Government's mission.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We need to have good laws on our statute books and the public must be able to enforce their legal rights in practice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, improving access to justice does not mean enabling vexatious litigants to mount abusive and unmeritorious legal claims.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There are existing levers to address the risk of abuse of process in specific contexts, which we regularly review.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For criminal proceedings, we passed legislation in 2018 and 2022, to provide clear procedures for applications filed after a concluded criminal appeal, including post-appeal applications in capital cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Thresholds were included to make clear that such late-stage applications must be premised on persuasive, new material to guard against persistent delays and the constant re-litigation of issues in criminal matters.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There are also existing levers available in other proceedings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For instance, the Protection from Harassment Court has powers to deal with unmeritorious or frivolous cases by striking out such claims and imposing costs consequences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, we have received feedback that there is still a risk of harassment proceedings being misused for collateral purposes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As such, this is an area we continue to monitor and review.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Similarly, for community disputes, the CDRT may award costs in cases involving an abuse of process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Under the Community Disputes Resolution (Amendment) Bill, which was passed yesterday, the Tribunal will be further empowered to issue civil restraint orders to curb claims or applications that are an abuse of process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: More broadly, the AOJPA provides that interference with court proceedings, or the administration of justice may amount to contempt of court and attract criminal sanctions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is a general protection that applies to all court proceedings in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The impact of egregious abuse of our court system can be serious, very serious.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Individuals are forced to bear the financial and psychological burden of undergoing court proceedings for matters that should not be going to court.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Limited public and court resources are diverted away from other deserving, meritorious cases and our court system is strained and weakened as a result.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: If we do not act, over time, trust in Singapore's justice system will be eroded.

speaker: The Minister of State for Law (Mr Murali Pillai) (for the Minister for Law)
text: We have observed notable examples of abuse of the court process in Singapore and overseas, as parties engage in what is referred to as "lawfare", commencing unmeritorious claims to oppress others or for ulterior purposes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL App.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In the handout, you will see that in the United States (US), lawfare has taken various forms.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This includes misuse of court proceedings by individuals against their intimate partners, who may be survivors of domestic violence or sexual abuse, as a means of controlling, harassing or intimidating them long after the relationship has ended.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It also includes unscrupulous lawyers and litigants commencing abusive or bogus claims with the main incentive of forcing a monetary settlement or to "make a quick buck".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In Europe, the European Union parliament is studying the rising phenomenon of strategic lawsuits against public participation, also known as "SLAPPs".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: SLAPPs are legal actions, typically brought with the intention of harassing or intimidating opponents via improper use of the legal system for purposes other than genuinely vindicating a legal right.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The United Kingdom (UK) government also proposed legislative action in this area earlier this year in March 2024.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In Singapore, we have also observed notable cases of egregious abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In an extra-judicial lecture delivered in 2023, our Chief Justice spoke about the phenomenon of truth decay: the proliferation of disinformation and devaluation of truth in our societies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He observed that "a number of recent examples suggest that truth decay is spreading into court proceedings".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He cited "the conduct of some advocates, who have in some cases attempted to conceal facts from the courts, or to delay proceedings on spurious grounds." One example of such conduct is the 2022 case of Mohammad Farid bin Batra v Attorney-General.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The applicant had been sentenced to life imprisonment and caning for possessing drugs for the purposes of trafficking.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: After his appeal had been dealt with, he filed two subsequent applications to the Court of Appeal, which were dismissed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Thereafter, the applicant filed another application to the General Division of the High Court on an urgent basis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In doing so, the Court found that the claim was completely baseless and brought to delay, and ultimately avoid, caning.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Court also noted that it "would have to leave it to the Executive and the Legislature to consider whether and what action can be taken in future instances of abusive applications by litigants and those advising, assisting or egging them on." Having observed these trends, we have decided that it is time to proactively act to safeguard the administration of justice in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is the Government's responsibility to act to protect the judicial system, especially when we have repeated pronouncements from our courts on the abuse of their processes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The current provisions of the AOJPA, in principle, already cover egregious abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Specifically, section 3(1)(e) of the AOJPA, which relates to contempt by interference with the administration of justice, captures: "Any person who…intentionally does any…act that interferes with, obstructs or poses a real risk of interference with or obstruction of the administration of justice …if the person knows or ought to have known that the act would interfere with, obstruct or pose a real risk of interference with or obstruction of the administration of justice." However, the language of the current provision, which I have just read, is broad.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We have decided that the legal position can be made clearer on how the general standard set out in section 3(1)(e) applies to the context of abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Besides providing legal clarity, our intent is also to send a clear signal to deter abuse of the court process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is also in line with the established legal position in other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In the UK, the Supreme Court has emphasised that serious cases of abuse of process involving false claims ought to be sanctioned as contempt of court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Court noted that such claims undermine the system in a number of serious ways, including imposing a burden upon honest claimants and damaging the system of adversarial justice which depends upon openness, transparency and honesty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Indian Supreme Court has also recognised that abuse of process that is calculated to hamper the due course of judicial proceedings or the orderly administration of justice amounts to contempt of court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Court noted that such conduct extends its influence beyond the parties to the action and affects the public's interest in the administration of justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Having set out the background and the policy rationale, I will now take hon Members through the details of the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The key point to note is that the provisions reflect what is already the current law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Under clause 2 of the Bill, the proposed new sections 3(1)(da) and (db) of the Act clarify what kinds of conduct would amount to contempt by interference with the administration of justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Three categories of egregious abuse of process are set out: first, the conduct or commencement of a court proceeding, which the person knows, or ought to have known, involves a deception on the court, is fictitious or constitutes a mere sham.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Second, the conduct or commencement of a court proceeding, which the person knows or ought to have known is manifestly groundless or without foundation and involves the process of the court being used for an ulterior or improper purpose.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Under this category, it is not sufficient just to have a manifestly groundless claim, or to have found an improper purpose.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Third, the conducting or commencing of multiple or successive court proceedings, which the person knows or ought to have known are manifestly groundless or without foundation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Deceiving the court, abusing the court process by filing baseless claims for an improper purpose, or launching multiple baseless court proceedings – these are acts of abuse that are clearly egregious and which cannot be condoned.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: These are also acts which would already fall within the current section 3(1)(e) of the AOJPA, as acts which interfere with the administration of justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Our amendments, therefore, do not change the current legal standard.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Rather, they provide clearer signposting in setting out the types of conduct that would amount to contempt of court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We have also considered that there may be also persons, who are causing or abetting others, to engage in the contemptuous conduct before our courts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The usual levers of striking out and costs orders will not deter them, as they are not involved in the court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In developing these proposals, we were keenly aware of the need to strike a balance between the need to guard against abuse of process and the rights of litigants to ventilate genuine claims before the courts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Our policy intent is that litigants and lawyers who act with reasonable care and in good faith should not be penalised.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We looked at past examples of conduct which amounted to abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We also examined the leading case of Chee Siok Chin v MHA, where the Court had set out the categories of abuse of process at common law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The approach we have taken ensures that the amendments will not cover the typical case of a civil matter that is struck out for the sole reason that it has no merit.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Such cases can continue to be adequately dealt with by striking out and cost orders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Court will be able to examine the circumstances of the case, when considering whether the conduct constitutes contempt.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In scoping the proposals, we spoke to key stakeholders, including the Judiciary, to ensure that we achieved the right balance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We also spoke to members of the Bar on these amendments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There is consensus that lawyers must be held to high standards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: At the same time, some members of the Bar have expressed concern whether these amendments may discourage lawyers from taking up difficult cases and arguments, where the merits of the case or the evidence may be borderline or unclear.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: They ask whether the amendments will prevent them from robustly representing the interests of their clients.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The elements of the new provisions, particularly the mental element that the person must have "known or ought to have known" that the proceeding would amount to contempt, are consistent with the current section 3(1)(e) of the AOJPA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The new provisions are also consistent with the pre-AOJPA case law on other forms of contempt of court, under which it was not necessary to prove an intention to undermine public confidence in the administration of justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The new provisions do not affect the procedural protections under the existing AOJPA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Consent of the Attorney-General is also required under section 30 of the AOJPA before contempt proceedings are instituted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Second, lawyers and litigants are already held to high standards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To reiterate, those who exercise reasonable care and act in good faith will not be caught and have nothing to fear.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: An accused person who has been convicted and had his appeal dismissed approaches a lawyer, shortly before the accused is to start serving his sentence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The accused presents new evidence that the lawyer is unsure whether is genuine.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The lawyer needs more time to investigate the matter and makes an urgent court application so that the accused person does not have to immediately start serving sentence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Eventually, after due investigation, it transpires that the allegedly new evidence is not genuine and the application is duly withdrawn.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In such a circumstance, if the lawyer had acted in good faith and had taken reasonable steps before filing the court application, considering the limited time available to him, the lawyer will not be caught by the elements of the proposed amendments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is because the standard of what the lawyer knew or ought to have known is contextual and the Court will have to examine carefully the factual matrix of each case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Rightly so, as we expect high standards from lawyers who owe paramount duties as officers of the Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Again, much will depend on the particular context of each case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is why I say that lawyers and litigants who act with reasonable care, and in good faith, have nothing to fear.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: On this point, as hon Members sitting in this House, we are ultimately concerned with the public good and must act in the best interest of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As I mentioned at the start of my speech, our justice system is a key pillar of what has made our country successful.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: All of us – the Courts, lawyers, lawmakers and members of the public – have an interest in ensuring that we have an effective justice system that is focused on enforcing our laws and resolving genuine disputes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We also have a duty to ensure that our processes are not weaponised or abused.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I have also taken some time to explain the rationale behind the amendments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, there were the two claims filed by a spurned boyfriend, which a Court found were commenced with the ulterior motive of pressuring a girlfriend not to terminate the relationship.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, there was a criminal case where a convicted drug trafficker was found to have filed a meritless court application for the purpose of delaying his sentence of caning till he reached 50 years of age when he could not be legally caned, the Farid Batra case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This case was referred to by the Minister of State earlier and is also listed in the handout that he distributed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since then, he has filed several applications for review of his conviction, as well as to bring a prisoner to Court, which were dismissed by the Court of Appeal either as speculative or an abuse of process.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the latest application in 2022, he applied for permission to commence a judicial review on the basis that a co-accused person should have faced an additional charge and received a heavier punishment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Court found that Mr Farid Batra did not have sufficient interest to start that action and that his real purpose was to delay his sentence of caning till he passed his 50th birthday and could not be caned.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Judge there expressed frustration that he did not have any options to punish Farid Batra for his abuse of court process, as he was a prisoner already serving life imprisonment, for whom there was no downside in mounting meritless applications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Court further stated that he "would leave it to the Executive and Legislature to consider whether and what action can be taken in future instances of abusive applications by litigants and those advising, assisting or egging them on".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, there appears to be a gap that needs to be addressed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would also be a contempt if the proceeding is manifestly groundless and involves the process of the court being employed for an ulterior or improper purpose.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Farid Batra's case appears to possibly fall within this provision.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this light, I have four queries on the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Two years ago, Parliament passed the Post-Appeal Applications and Capital Cases Act, or PACC, which came into effect in June this year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under PACC, strict conditions have been imposed on when additional applications can be made to the Court in capital cases where the usual avenues of appeal have been exhausted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As this Act has just been operationalised, it is only fair to wait and see whether it is adequate to manage court proceedings in capital cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill provides a factual scenario in Illustration 4 where the offender is convicted of rape, which is a non-capital offence.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is this an indication that the provisions are really targeted at non-capital cases?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As mentioned earlier, Farid Batra was sentenced to jail for life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even if he were to be convicted for contempt of court, an additional jail term imposed may not have any deterrent effect.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will the new contempt provisions discourage the filing of meritless applications in such situations?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: No doubt, the use of lawfare to oppress defendants is a concern.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, MinLaw recognises that there are existing court procedures that enable typical civil cases to be struck out for lacking merit and for the losing party to be ordered to pay legal costs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, where do we draw the line as to which cases are tantamount to a contempt of court and which are better off being dealt with by the usual rules of civil procedure?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One must remember that contempt of court is a very serious matter which carries a heavy punishment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, these provisions must not be triggered lightly and the bar must be set very high.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MinLaw has stated that the contempt law will not cover cases where litigants and lawyers have acted with reasonable care and good faith.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Neither should the contempt laws be invoked in cases where existing procedures to deal with the situation are adequate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Would it not be preferable to codify these carve-outs so as to give further confidence to those acting in good faith?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Here, I declare that I am an advocate and solicitor.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As we know, lawyers are officers of the Court and already subject to the control of the Supreme Court through the Legal Profession Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We see this disciplinary aspect exercised every day in various ways.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, whenever lawyers are assessed by the Court to have conducted a case in a way that amounts to an abuse of the court process, the Court may order them to pay costs personally, that is, out of their own pockets.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Alternatively, lawyers are periodically referred by the Courts or the Attorney-General to face disciplinary proceedings for any misconduct.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The outcome of such proceedings could be a striking of the role, suspension, financial penalties and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier in the handout, the Minister of State highlighted an extrajudicial lecture by the Chief Justice where he spoke about truth decay and how lawyers might be complicit in that process.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But it is not clear from the extract that the Chief Justice was actually calling for additional measures against lawyers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like the Minister of State to clarify this point.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These abuses squander public resources and judicial time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They also hurt genuine victims who need fair and prompt resolutions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am confident that the provisions in this Bill will booster the integrity of our judicial system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I endorse the intent and spirit of this legislation, I would like to seek further clarifications on four key areas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I support the need to curb abusive litigation, we must be careful not to discourage individuals with genuine grievances from seeking justice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must deter bad faith actors without dissuading those with sincere, if ultimately unsuccessful, claims.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Take for instance, a recent case under current contempt laws.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A blogger was charged with contempt for making unfounded accusations against the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He implied that the Judiciary was swayed by the Government.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Court found that his statements had the potential to erode public trust in our Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe this case was ultimately shown to be a good use of the law.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It highlights the fine line we tread between maintaining the integrity of our Courts and protecting freedom of expression.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Addressing harmful and unsubstantiated allegations is undoubtedly important.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could these legislations deter residents, especially those with limited legal knowledge, from exercising their right to justice?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And might these amendments dissuade pro bono lawyers from supporting disadvantaged residents due to potential repercussions?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is essential that as we curb misuse of the Court's time, we do not inadvertently silence legitimate cries for justice due to fears of unintended legal consequences.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Stricter contempt provisions may disproportionately affect those who face financial or legal challenges, as they may feel the chilling effects of these amendments most acutely.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Navigating the legal system can be daunting, even for those with resources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The risk of contempt charges may discourage self-represented litigants, especially those with sincere claims, from coming forward.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will these amendments protect those who lack the resources to fully understand legal complexities?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, how can community legal clinics and support services help mitigate this risk for residents?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Ensuring access to justice requires that we balance curbing misuse while maintaining protections for the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is essential to uphold equitable access to our legal system for all residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Accountability is vital, but we must consider how this might affect lawyers' willingness to take up pro bono or challenging cases, particularly those with a public interest angle but uncertain outcomes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A case in 2022 illustrates this dilemma, where two lawyers were ordered to pay personal costs due to their conduct in a case.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Their approach was deemed problematic as they introduced evidence piecemeal and at the last minute.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These examples highlight the tension lawyers may face when advocating passionately for their clients.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Court's reaction highlights the necessity of adhering to procedural rules.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, it is also important to acknowledge that in critical cases, legal counsel might be driven to explore every possible option to advert potential miscarriages of justice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What recourse will residents have if they feel their lawyer has not accurately represented the risk of contempt under this amendment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clarity is essential, not only for those seeking justice, but also for the legal professionals who guide them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will help ensure fair, accessible and equitable representation for all.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the amendments are well-intentioned, they could unintentionally create a sense of reduced access to justice amongst the public.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Maintaining public confidence in our Court's accessibility and fairness is paramount.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The blogger case I mentioned earlier sparked considerable debates, both locally and internationally, on freedom of expression and fairness in our legal system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Human rights organisations and international media outlets cited the case as an example of perceived suppression of free speech.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This shows that striking a balance between upholding respect for the Judiciary and preserving public trust is not only delicate but essential.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, what steps will the Government take to ensure these changes do not undermine public confidence in our justice system?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could more detailed public reporting on cases deemed manifestly groundless help clarify the rationale for these amendments?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Transparency in how these provisions are applied could reinforce the public's understanding and trust in the system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A just society is built not only on the laws we enact, but on the public's trust in those laws and their fair and transparent application.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe these amendments will reinforce the backbone of our legal system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But to ensure its full impact, we must address the potential challenges it brings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the amendments are intended to prevent abuse of judicial processes through frivolous and vexatious litigation, we should also minimise any potentially unimpeded impact.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on what constitutes deception of the court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is fair litigation strategy to commence court proceedings even if a party's intention is to amicably settle the matter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Starting court proceedings is a commonly used tactic to signal to the other party the seriousness and strength of the other party's case.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Commencing court proceedings with the intention of settling the case could be, in the strictest sense, a deception of the court or fictitious, in the sense that the party had no intention of seeing the proceedings all the way through to trial.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State elaborate on how it would distinguish between cases that would be deemed deception of the court and the use of court proceedings as part of fair litigation strategy?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on what constitutes court proceedings that are manifestly groundless or without foundation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not unusual for lawyers and their clients to disagree on whether certain claims have merit or are supported by evidence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In certain cases, clients might instruct their lawyers to proceed with claims, even if they have been advised that the claims are weak.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In other cases, clients may instruct their lawyers to file claims in the hope that more evidence will emerge through discovery to support their initially unsupported claims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are existing mechanisms, such as striking out and cost orders, to deal with unmeritorious claims.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, as MinLaw has clarified, the amendments are not intended to cover typical cases that are struck out for the reason that it has no merit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State clarify the qualitative difference between a case that is manifestly groundless or without foundation and a case that simply has no merit?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that the test is that the individual know or ought to know, the standard is an objective one.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Uncertainty on how the objective test is set leads to the concerns of parties pursuing an aggressive litigation strategy, unwittingly committing contempt of court.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final point is on the expansion of contempt liability to non-parties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister of State provide specific examples of influence by third parties that fall under the scope of section 3(7)?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not unusual for litigants to seek advice and support from acquaintances and advisors on the conduct of their litigation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 3(7) may cause these well-meaning individuals to be fearful of providing much needed support for litigants to pursue justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I am heartened that hon Members agree on the importance of safeguarding our court system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Before I respond to the specific questions, let me reiterate a key point which I made in my opening speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The primary effect of the amendments is to signpost the types of abuse of process which would amount to contempt of court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Some of the questions posed by hon Members assume that the Bill makes our contempt of court laws stricter or tighter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I ask hon Members to keep this broader point in mind, as I provide my responses to the specific questions raised.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I start with the balance between promoting access to justice and the need to deter abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how the amendments might affect those with valid grievances, including vulnerable residents and self-represented persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He also asked whether the amendments could create a sense of reduced access to justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Government, as hon Members would be aware, has taken significant steps in recent years to improve access to justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I spoke about some of these steps in my opening speech, such as the setting up of specialised Courts with simplified processes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Needy Singaporeans can also access legal aid through the Legal Aid Bureau and the Public Defender's Office.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We also work closely with partners, like ProBono SG, to promote access to justice in the community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This includes supporting ProBono SG in setting up community law centres in the heartlands – at the Tian De Temple in Hougang last year and in the Realm of Tranquility in Woodlands earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: If any member of our community has a genuine claim and requires legal assistance, there are resources available.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Rather, they are targeted at egregious abuses of the court processes, such as the filing of fictitious claims or commencing baseless proceedings motivated by an improper purpose.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: One does not need to be a lawyer to know that such conduct is wrong.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I should add that deterring abuse of process and promoting access to justice are, in fact, complementary goals.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is because abusive claims drain the limited resources of our Judiciary, thereby reducing access to justice for genuine litigants.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In other words, deterring abusive claims is necessary to maintaining access to justice and public trust in the legal system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Next, I move on to the specific issues raised by hon Members.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked what kinds of cases this Bill is targeted at.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As I have stated earlier, the Bill will apply to all cases before our Singapore Courts, including criminal and civil cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim also noted that there are some persons, such as offenders serving a life sentence, who would see no "downside" in making multiple court applications.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We acknowledge that the deterrent effect of the amendments may be limited in such cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: However, in the case of Mohammad Farid bin Batra v Attorney-General, which the hon Member mentioned, the Court also referred to third parties who advised, assisted or egged on the offenders to commit such conduct, and these amendments are still important to deter such persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I next turn to questions raised on the legal elements of the new provisions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked what constitutes deception on the court and the definition of the phrase "manifestly groundless or without foundation".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: These phrases are based on the current case law on abuse of process, and the leading case of Chee Siok Chin v MHA, as I mentioned earlier in my speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It would not be possible for me to make detailed pronouncements on how these standards should be applied by the Courts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Whether these thresholds are met will depend on the particular facts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: On the ground of deception on the court, the cases that have been found to have transgressed this limb typically involve egregious conduct, such as claims which are founded on a fictitious factual premise.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To put it simply, where the claim is based on a falsehood.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Our intention is not to capture fair litigation strategy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is something for the Court to assess in each case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There must be other abusive factors present, such as the bringing of the claim for an improper purpose under the new section 3(1)(da)(ii) or the filing of multiple or successive claims under the new section 3(1)(db).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is the reason why I stated in my opening speech earlier that the amendments are not intended to cover the typical case that is struck out for the sole reason that it has no merit.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member Mr Zhulkarnain asked about section 3(1)(db).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The section covers the conduct of multiple or successive proceedings which the person knows or ought to have known is manifestly groundless or without foundation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Specifically, Mr Zhulkarnain asked why the section does not also contain the requirement that the proceedings would cause "improper vexation or oppression".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As I explained in my opening speech, the provisions in the Bill are different from the categories of abuse of process at common law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We have carefully scoped our proposals to capture egregious abuses of process that would interfere with, or obstruct, our administration of justice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is conduct that would already be captured under the current section 3(1)(e) of the AOJPA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But our amendments provide clarity on how the general standard applies to specific contexts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In particular, the purpose of the new section 3(1)(db) is to address the harm to the court system, as a whole, caused when a person files multiple or successive proceedings that are manifestly groundless.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: A multiplicity of such baseless proceedings diverts precious resources away from deserving cases and the harm is not limited to the vexation or oppression of the other party.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In addition, there could be other culpable motivations for a person to file multiple or successive proceedings besides improper vexation or oppression.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: For instance, the person may file successive baseless claims to delay proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Again, this is harmful to our administration of justice, which ought to be deterred.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member, Mr Zhulkarnain, observed that third parties can already be liable for contempt in certain circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He asked whether the new section 3(7), which covers persons who cause or abet abusive conduct represents a change in the current position.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As with the other new provisions, section 3(7) is clarificatory in nature.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In particular, section 3(1)(e) of the Act already covers "any person" who does "any other act that interferes with, obstructs or poses a real risk of interference with or obstruction of the administration of justice in any other manner".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This may include persons who cause or abet other forms of contempt of court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Hon Members Mr Louis Ng and Mr Zhulkarnain also asked about the scope of third-party liability.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether the amendments may inadvertently capture well-meaning individuals.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain also asked if the provisions would extend to those who fund frivolous actions, including members of the public who participate in crowdfunding.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To give an example, this would cover third parties who instigate others to commit egregious abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The Court will examine the particular facts, including what the non-party knew or ought to have known, when considering whether the non-party is liable for contempt of court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I next turn to the impact of the amendments on lawyers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Hon Member, Mr Yip Hon Weng, asked whether there could be guidelines on what lawyers ought to know when assessing the merits of a case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain suggested a carve-out if the lawyer advises his client that he or she has a bad case, but the client nevertheless instructs the lawyer to proceed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As Mr Zhulkarnain rightly noted in his speech, lawyers are already held to high professional standards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: They owe paramount duties as officers of the Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: They are also bound by obligations under the Professional Conduct Rules.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Thus, we are not changing the standards that lawyers need to uphold when dealing with clients or assessing the merits of the case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Where the client insists on proceeding with an abusive claim against the lawyer's advice, the standards and expectations are clear.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As the Court of Three Judges noted in a recent disciplinary proceeding, the duty of the lawyer is, and I quote: "to dispense his professional duties with moral courage and independence in the face of pressures from his clients.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is open to the solicitor to inform his client of the conflicting duty on account of the instructions and, if necessary, to discharge himself from acting for the client." The fact that the client insists on proceeding is not, and cannot be, an excuse for the lawyer to commit an egregious abuse of process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member, Ms Sylvia Lim, asked why the existing levers available for lawyers, including disciplinary proceedings, are inadequate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Disciplinary proceedings and contempt proceedings serve different purposes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Contempt of court serves a broader purpose than other levers, as it is aimed at protecting our justice system as a whole.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Thus, contempt proceedings are instituted by the state, unlike the other levers, which are sought by individuals in the case of cost orders, or professional bodies in the case of disciplinary actions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Proceedings for contempt of court, which carry criminal sanctions, are also meant to protect the administration of justice, which goes beyond just one case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim also suggested that it should be codified in the Bill that provisions do not cover persons who act with reasonable care and good faith.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It is inherent in the elements of the provisions that such persons would not be caught in line with our policy intent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In cases where a person acted with actual knowledge, then it is self-evident, they could not have acted in good faith.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, in a sense, we are ad idem on the net effect, because the point about codifying a defence is already embedded in the ingredients provided for in the amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain also suggested having a database of frivolous litigants and that the public be provided with more information on the resources and costs involved in such cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As I mentioned in my opening speech, key stakeholders were consulted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: These include the Judiciary and the Attorney-General’s Chambers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: We also spoke with the representatives from the Law Society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And as I mentioned in my speech, there were also concerns from some lawyers as to whether these amendments will hamper them from doing their best for their clients, particularly in difficult cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I promised them I would deal with their concerns in my opening speech and that is what I did.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Conversations like these help us find the appropriate balance to promote an effective justice system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: That is why we have regular, ongoing, conversations with our key stakeholders, including the members of the Bar.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As always, the Ministry is open to further feedback on our policies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: With that, Sir, I conclude my round up speech and I once again thank the hon Members again for their support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I shall put the question to the House.      .

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 4.05 pm until 4.30 pm.
